description: Pocket Science Lab (PSLab) & EspoTek Labrador Comprehensive Engineering Knowledge Base for RAG context retrieval.

documents.title: PSLab Instruments Catalog & System Overview
documents.content:
Pocket Science Lab (PSLab) is an open-source hardware and software extension developed by FOSSASIA that turns computers and mobile devices into a full-featured science laboratory and electronics workbench. The PSLab mobile and desktop application supports two distinct open-source hardware boards:
1. Official PSLab Board (V5 & V6): Powered by a 16-bit Microchip PIC24 microcontroller, offering 4-channel oscilloscope, digital multimeter, dual arbitrary wave generators, 4 programmable DC power rails, 4-channel logic analyzer, I2C/SPI/UART buses, and dedicated ESP-01 Wi-Fi header.
2. EspoTek Labrador Board: Powered by an Atmel ATXMEGA32A4U microcontroller, offering a 2-channel 750kSPS oscilloscope, digital multimeter, 1MSPS arbitrary wave generator, 2-channel power supply (+12V/-12V), and 3MSPS logic analyzer.
The app includes 16 built-in virtual instruments:
1. Oscilloscope: Multi-channel real-time waveform capture (CH1, CH2, CH3, and host MIC), FFT frequency spectra, XY Lissajous plots, and edge triggering.
2. Multimeter: High-precision voltage, resistance, capacitance, frequency, and continuity testing.
3. Wave Generator: Dual analog DAC waveform outputs (W1, W2) and four digital PWM square wave outputs (SQ1-SQ4).
4. Power Source: Programmable DC voltage rails (PV1: +/-5V, PV2: +/-3.3V, PV3: 0-3.3V) and constant current source (PCS: 0-3.3mA), or Labrador PSU (+12V/-12V).
5. Logic Analyzer: Multi-channel digital capture with protocol decoders for I2C, SPI, and UART.
6. Lux Meter: Ambient illuminance measurement in lux via phone sensor or BH1750/TSL2561.
7. Accelerometer: 3-axis motion and gravitational acceleration tracking (m/s^2 or g-force).
8. Barometer: Atmospheric air pressure (hPa) and barometric altitude estimation.
9. Compass / Magnetometer: Earth's geomagnetic field and azimuth compass heading.
10. Gyroscope: Angular rotational velocity tracking (deg/s).
11. Thermometer: Ambient and surface temperature measurement.
12. Sound Meter: Acoustic sound pressure measurement in decibels (dB SPL) with event classification.
13. Gas Sensor: Environmental air quality and combustible gas monitoring (MQ series).
14. Robotic Arm: Multi-axis servo motor PWM controller (SQ1-SQ4).
15. OLED Display: I2C-driven graphic display rendering (SSD1306).
16. Firmware Flasher: Built-in in-app updater for PSLab V6 PIC24 firmware, ESP-01 Wi-Fi firmware, and EspoTek Labrador firmware.
CONNECTIVITY & PLATFORM RULES: PSLab board connects via USB OTG (PC and Android) or Wi-Fi (via the onboard ESP-01 module). PSLab does NOT support Bluetooth. iOS devices (iPhones & iPads) can ONLY connect to the official PSLab board wirelessly via Wi-Fi with an ESP-01 module. EspoTek Labrador does NOT support iOS under any circumstances (Labrador is strictly USB-only and lacks Wi-Fi; Apple iOS strictly blocks generic USB host communication). Firmware flashing is NOT supported on iOS for any device.
CRITICAL FIRMWARE FLASHING RULES: Firmware flashing is NOT supported on iOS (Apple's ecosystem strictly blocks raw USB serial OTG communication and DFU bootloader control). Firmware flashing can ONLY be used on Android, Desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux), and Web via a direct physical USB cable (USB OTG adapter on Android, standard USB cable on PC/Web). Firmware flashing CANNOT be performed wirelessly over Wi-Fi.

documents.title: PSLab Hardware Design, Schematics, and Pinout Architecture
documents.content:
Official PSLab Hardware Architecture (based on fossasia/pslab-hardware schematics for V5 and V6 revisions):
• Microcontroller (MCU): Microchip PIC24EP256GP204 (16-bit, 70 MIPS, 256 KB Flash, 32 KB SRAM, 10/12-bit high-speed ADC with DMA, hardware timers, and Output Compare PWM peripherals).
• USB Serial Bridge: Silicon Labs CP2102 or WCH CH340 USB-to-UART transceiver (or native PIC24 USB on specific revisions) communicating at high baud rates (e.g. 1,000,000 baud or 115,200 baud).
• Analog Front-End (AFE):
  - Programmable Gain Amplifiers (PGAs): Microchip MCP6S21 SPI PGAs provide software-selectable input gains (1x, 2x, 4x, 5x, 8x, 10x, 16x, 32x) on oscilloscope channels CH1 and CH2, enabling measurement ranges from +/-16.5V down to +/-500mV.
  - Analog Multiplexer: NXP 74HC4051 8-channel analog mux routes auxiliary signals, voltmeter inputs, and internal diagnostic loops to the PIC24 ADC.
  - Operational Amplifiers: Quad rail-to-rail op-amps (LMV324 / TLV272 / MCP6004) buffer input signals, scale DAC outputs, and drive the constant current source.
  - Input Protection: Fast-clamping Schottky diodes and 1 MOhm input impedance protect analog inputs against overvoltage up to +/-30V.
• Power Supply Subsystem:
  - Input: 5V DC from USB VBUS (or external 5V on Vin header).
  - Analog Rails: Inverting charge pump / switching inverters generate a stable -5V negative rail, enabling true bipolar operation (+/-5V on PV1, +/-3.3V on PV2, and negative voltage deflection on CH1/CH2).
  - LDO Regulators: 3.3V low-dropout regulators supply clean power to the PIC24, external I2C sensors, and the ESP-01 Wi-Fi module.
• Digital-to-Analog Converters (DACs):
  - 12-bit DACs generate analog waveforms W1, W2 and DC rails PV1, PV2, PV3, PCS.
  - Hardware Relationship: PV1 and PV3 share DAC reference architecture and scale proportionally; PV2 and PCS are inversely proportional.
• Built-in ESP-01 Wi-Fi Header: Dedicated 2x4 (8-pin) socket connected directly to PIC24 hardware UART (TX/RX) and GPIO pins for software-controlled reset and flashing.

documents.title: PSLab ESP-01 Wi-Fi Module & Wireless Architecture
documents.content:
PSLab Wi-Fi Hardware & Wireless Architecture (fossasia/pslab-esp01-firmware):
• Wireless Mechanism: PSLab uses an Espressif ESP8266 ESP-01 module (or ESP32 equivalent) plugged into the dedicated 8-pin ESP-01 socket on the PSLab board. IMPORTANT: PSLab does NOT have Bluetooth. The board communicates strictly via USB or Wi-Fi.
• Firmware Requirement: To support wireless operation, the ESP-01 module must be flashed with the dedicated 'pslab-esp01-firmware' (available on GitHub: fossasia/pslab-esp01-firmware or via the PSLab app's built-in Firmware Flasher).
• Network Operating Modes:
  1. Access Point (AP Mode): Default configuration. The ESP-01 creates its own autonomous Wi-Fi network (SSID: 'PSLab' or 'PSLab-XXXX'). The phone or PC connects directly to this network without needing a router.
  2. Station Mode (STA Mode): Connects to an existing home or lab Wi-Fi network.
• Communication Protocol: The ESP-01 runs a high-throughput transparent bridge between TCP socket port 1234 (default IP: 192.168.4.1) and the PIC24 hardware UART at 1,000,000 baud. All command packets and waveform buffers stream bidirectionally over TCP/IP or WebSocket.
• Mobile Compatibility: Android and PCs can use either USB OTG or Wi-Fi. iPhones and iPads CANNOT connect via USB (due to iOS USB serial driver restrictions) and MUST connect wirelessly via Wi-Fi with the ESP-01 module installed.
• Flashing Restriction: While the ESP-01 module provides wireless telemetry for instruments, firmware flashing CANNOT be performed over Wi-Fi. Flashing requires a direct physical USB cable connection on Android, Desktop, or Web. iOS does NOT support firmware flashing.

documents.title: EspoTek Labrador Board Architecture & PSLab App Integration
documents.content:
EspoTek Labrador Hardware Architecture & PSLab Integration:
• Overview: EspoTek Labrador is an open-source USB multi-tool supported natively by the PSLab application. It is powered by an Atmel/Microchip ATXMEGA32A4U 8/16-bit microcontroller running at 32 MHz with native Full-Speed USB (USB VID 0x03EB, PID 0xBA94).
• CRITICAL PLATFORM COMPATIBILITY - iOS IS NOT SUPPORTED: EspoTek Labrador does NOT support iOS devices (iPhones or iPads). Because Apple's operating system strictly blocks raw USB host communication and bulk transfers, and the Labrador board does NOT have an ESP-01 Wi-Fi module (it is strictly USB-only), Labrador CANNOT be used on iOS under any circumstances. Labrador is supported ONLY on Android (via USB OTG), Desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux via USB), and Web (via WebUSB/WebSerial). Neither instruments nor firmware flashing for Labrador work on iOS.
• Oscilloscope Subsystem:
  - 2 Analog Input Channels (CH1, CH2).
  - Sampling Rate: Up to 750 kSPS dual-channel simultaneous capture, or 1.5 MSPS single-channel.
  - Voltage Range: -12V to +12V (or +/-20V with probe attenuation), 8-bit ADC resolution.
• Digital Multimeter Subsystem:
  - Measures DC voltage, AC voltage (RMS), current, and resistance (Ohmmeter).
• Waveform Generator Subsystem:
  - 1 Analog Output Channel driven by an internal 12-bit 1 MSPS DAC.
  - Generates Sine, Triangle, Sawtooth, and Square waves up to 50 kHz with configurable amplitude and DC offset.
• Dual Power Supply (PSU Subsystem):
  - Positive Rail (PSU+): Software-controlled boost converter providing +4.5V up to +12.0V DC.
  - Negative Rail (PSU-): Inverting charge pump providing -4.5V down to -12.0V DC.
  - Current Capability: ~150 mA per rail directly from USB power.
• Logic Analyzer Subsystem:
  - 2 to 4 digital channels sampling up to 3 MSPS with edge-triggered capture.
• PSLab App Driver & Firmware:
  - The app connects via native USB bulk transfer endpoints using firmware variant 'labrafirm_000c_03.hex'.
  - When connected, the app detects the Labrador board, adapts UI channel selectors, and routes commands through LabradorHardwareBoard.
• Flashing Support: Labrador firmware can be flashed using the built-in Firmware Flasher exclusively on Android, Desktop, and Web via direct physical USB cable. Firmware flashing is NOT supported on iOS.

documents.title: Firmware Flasher Screen (PSLab V6, ESP-01 Wi-Fi, EspoTek Labrador)
documents.content:
The PSLab application includes a built-in 'Firmware Update' (Firmware Flasher) screen accessible from the navigation drawer:
• PLATFORM SUPPORT & RESTRICTIONS:
  - iOS IS NOT SUPPORTED: Firmware flashing is completely unsupported on iOS devices (iPhones & iPads). Apple's operating system strictly restricts raw USB OTG serial access and DFU bootloader flashing.
  - Supported Platforms: Firmware flashing can ONLY be used on Android, Desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux), and Web (WebUSB / WebSerial).
  - USB Cable Only: Flashing requires a direct physical USB cable connection (USB OTG adapter on Android, standard USB-A/C cable on Desktop and Web).
  - Wi-Fi Flashing NOT Supported: Firmware flashing CANNOT be performed wirelessly over Wi-Fi. Microcontroller bootloaders (PIC24 bootloader, Atmel DFU, and ESP-01 serial programming) require physical hardware reset and low-level serial synchronization.
• Supported Target Devices:
  1. PSLab V6: Flashes the PIC24 microcontroller firmware. Supports downloading official releases directly from GitHub (fossasia/pslab-firmware) or loading custom local .hex files. Guides the user through entering Bootloader mode.
  2. ESP-01 Wi-Fi Module: Flashes the wireless bridge firmware (fossasia/pslab-esp01-firmware) to the 8-pin ESP-01 module via the board's serial bridge.
  3. EspoTek Labrador: Flashes the ATXMEGA32A4U microcontroller. Includes built-in firmware variants:
     - labrafirm_000c_03.hex: Variant 03 (Bulk USB Transfer - recommended for high-speed streaming in this app).
     - labrafirm_0007_01.hex / labrafirm_0007_02.hex: Legacy Isochronous streaming variants.
     - Local .hex file selection for experimental builds.
  - Bootloader Jump: The flasher can send a software command to jump a connected Labrador board directly into DFU bootloader mode without requiring manual button presses.

documents.title: PSLab Host Microphone Input (MIC Channel)
documents.content: The MIC channel on the PSLab Oscilloscope samples acoustic audio signals directly using the host device's operating system audio subsystem (computer built-in microphone, smartphone microphone, or 3.5mm headset jack). It utilizes host OS audio drivers and operates completely independently of the physical PSLab hardware board. Even when the PSLab USB board status is 'Disconnected / Standby', the MIC channel captures REAL LIVE acoustic audio from the host device's microphone, NOT simulated test data. Typical ambient sound and speech produce small amplitudes (Vpp approx 0.01V to 0.2V) and frequencies from 50 Hz to 4000 Hz. Because the default oscilloscope voltage scale is wide (+/- 16V), acoustic microphone waveforms appear small or flat near 0V on screen unless zoomed in.

documents.title: Oscilloscope Hardware Channels & Signal Sources
documents.content:
The PSLab Oscilloscope provides four input channels with distinct hardware mappings:
• CH1 (Analog Pin): Programmable gain amplifier with ranges +/-16.5V down to +/-0.5V, 1 MOhm input impedance, and software-switchable AC/DC coupling.
• CH2 (Analog Pin): Programmable gain range +/-16.5V down to +/-0.5V, 1 MOhm input impedance.
• CH3 (Analog Pin): High-speed unipolar ADC channel (0 to 3.3V range).
• MIC (Host Audio Subsystem): Samples audio directly from the host computer or phone's built-in microphone / 3.5mm jack via host OS audio drivers. Crucially, MIC operates completely independently of the physical PSLab board. Even when the board is disconnected or in simulation mode, the MIC channel captures REAL LIVE acoustic audio from the room. Typical ambient acoustic signals range from Vpp = 0.01V to 0.2V, 50 Hz to 4 kHz. To view acoustic waveforms clearly, decrease the voltage scale to +/- 0.5V or +/- 1V and set timebase to 1-10 ms/div.
• Labrador Mode: When an EspoTek Labrador board is active, the oscilloscope operates with 2 analog channels (CH1, CH2) sampling at up to 750 kSPS across -12V to +12V.

documents.title: Oscilloscope Timebase, Triggering, FFT, and XY Plots
documents.content:
Oscilloscope analysis controls:
• Timebase: Horizontal sweep rate (ms/div). Fast sweep (< 1 ms/div) resolves high-frequency carrier waves (> 1 kHz). Slower sweep (> 20 ms/div) displays audio modulation, envelopes, or low-frequency sensor fluctuations.
• Trigger: Stabilizes repetitive periodic waveforms by initiating capture on a rising or falling edge threshold voltage. 'Free Run' continuously updates without synchronization, which may cause periodic signals to drift horizontally.
• Fourier Transform (FFT): Converts time-domain waveforms into frequency spectra, showing fundamental frequencies and harmonic distortions.
• XY Plot: Plots CH1 against CH2 instead of time, creating Lissajous patterns used to calculate phase angle differences: \(\sin(\Delta\phi) = \frac{y_0}{y_{\max}}\), and to determine frequency ratios between two oscillators.

documents.title: Digital Multimeter Architecture, Pins, and Ranges
documents.content:
The PSLab Digital Multimeter (DMM) routes measurements through dedicated hardware pins:
• Voltage: Measured on CH1 (+/-16.5V), CH2 (+/-16.5V), CH3 (0-3.3V), or the dedicated VOL pin (0-3.3V unipolar DC/AC RMS).
• Resistance (RES pin): Evaluated by injecting a calibrated constant current through the RES pin into the test component connected to GND and measuring the resulting voltage drop. Supported range: 100 Ohm to 100 kOhm.
• Capacitance (CAP pin): Measured by charging the capacitor through a known internal resistor and precisely timing the RC voltage curve transition to 63.2% of Vdd. Supported range: 5 pF to 100 uF.
• Frequency & Clock Pulses: Evaluated on digital logic pins (LA1 to LA4) up to 4 MHz with duty cycle tracking.
• Continuity: Verifies circuit paths under 50 Ohms with visual status and audible buzzer tone.
• Labrador Mode: Multimeter measures DC/AC Volts, Current, and Resistance via Labrador hardware AFE.

documents.title: Wave Generator Architecture (W1, W2, SQ1-SQ4 / PWM)
documents.content:
The PSLab Wave Generator provides dual analog outputs and quad digital outputs:
• Analog Channels (W1 / SI1 & W2 / SI2): Driven by internal 12-bit DACs. Capable of generating Sine, Triangular, or Sawtooth waveforms from 0.1 Hz up to 5000 Hz, with peak-to-peak amplitude up to 3.3V and configurable phase offset between W1 and W2.
• Digital Channels (SQ1 to SQ4 / SQR1 to SQR4): High-speed pulse-width modulation (PWM) outputs operating from 1 Hz up to 8 MHz with 0% to 100% programmable duty cycle.
• Self-Test Diagnostic Loop: Connecting a jumper wire from W1 to CH1 on the PSLab board allows instantaneous verification of DAC output and oscilloscope ADC sampling without external circuitry.
• Labrador Mode: Provides 1 analog output channel driven by a 1 MSPS 12-bit DAC generating Sine, Triangle, Square, and Sawtooth up to 50 kHz.

documents.title: Programmable DC Power Supplies (PV1, PV2, PV3, PCS & Labrador PSU)
documents.content:
The Power Source instrument controls the programmable DC outputs of the connected hardware:
• PSLab Board Rails:
  - PV1: Programmable bipolar DC supply with +/- 5.0V range adjustable in fine 5 mV steps. Ideal for analog op-amp circuits requiring positive and negative rails.
  - PV2: Programmable supply with +/- 3.3V range.
  - PV3: Programmable supply with 0 to +3.3V unipolar range (logic level reference).
  - PCS (Programmable Constant Current Source): Delivers 0 to 3.3 mA constant current, ideal for characterization of diode I-V curves, forward voltage drops, and sensor excitation.
  - Hardware Relationship Rules: In PSLab V5/V6, PV1 and PV3 outputs are proportional, while PV2 and PCS are inversely proportional due to shared DAC reference architecture.
• Labrador Board Power Supply (PSU):
  - Positive Rail (PSU+): Programmable boost output from +4.5V up to +12.0V.
  - Negative Rail (PSU-): Programmable inverting output from -4.5V down to -12.0V.
  - Delivers up to 150 mA per rail directly from USB power.

documents.title: Logic Analyzer Channels & Digital Protocol Decoding
documents.content:
The PSLab Logic Analyzer captures high-speed discrete digital signals:
• PSLab Channels: 4 Digital Channels (LA1, LA2, LA3, LA4), supporting 3.3V and 5V TTL/CMOS logic levels with DMA burst capture up to 64 MSa/s.
• Labrador Channels: 2 to 4 channels with sampling up to 3 MSa/s.
• Trigger Modes: Edge-triggered on rising edge, falling edge, every edge, or every 4th edge.
• Hardware Protocol Decoders: Built-in software protocol decoders for UART (serial RX/TX with custom baud rates), I2C (SCL clock on LA1, SDA data on LA2 with address/ACK framing), and SPI (SCK, MOSI, MISO, CS).

documents.title: Sensor Instruments (Lux, Accelerometer, Barometer, Compass, Gyro, Thermometer, Gas)
documents.content:
PSLab supports both built-in host device sensors and external plug-in I2C sensors:
• Lux Meter: Ambient illuminance (lux) using phone ambient sensor or BH1750/TSL2561 I2C modules.
• Accelerometer: Measures 3-axis acceleration (X, Y, Z in m/s^2 or g-force) using phone IMU or external MPU6050/ADXL345 sensors. Useful for studying gravity, tilt angle, vibration, and harmonic motion.
• Barometer: High-precision barometric pressure (hPa) using BMP180/BMP280/BME280 sensors, enabling barometric altimetry and elevation change tracking.
• Compass: 3-axis magnetometer measuring magnetic field strength (micro-Tesla) and computing magnetic north azimuth heading (0 to 360 degrees).
• Gyroscope: Angular velocity (deg/s) along pitch, roll, and yaw axes.
• Thermometer: Temperature measurement in Celsius/Fahrenheit using onboard thermistors or digital DS18B20/BME280 sensors.
• Gas Sensor: Measures concentration of volatile organic compounds, smoke, or gases using MQ series analog sensors connected to CH1 or CH3.
• Sound Meter: Real-time sound level intensity in decibels (dB SPL) via host microphone.

documents.title: Robotic Arm Servo Controller & OLED Display Modules
documents.content:
Specialized PSLab interface tools:
• Robotic Arm: Drives up to 4 analog hobby servo motors (e.g., SG90, MG90S) simultaneously using PSLab digital PWM pins (SQ1 to SQ4). Provides a 50 Hz (20 ms period) pulse width modulation signal, varying pulse width from 1.0 ms (0 degrees) to 2.0 ms (180 degrees) per servo joint (Base, Bicep, Forearm, Gripper).
• OLED Display: Renders custom text, sensor graphs, and bitmap graphics onto an external 0.96-inch 128x64 SSD1306 OLED display interfaced through the PSLab I2C header pins (SDA, SCL, VDD, GND).

documents.title: Experiment: Acoustic Sound Analysis with Microphone & Oscilloscope
documents.content:
Experiment Guide: Acoustic Sound Analysis
Goal: Measure ambient room sound, human voice, or tuning fork tone frequencies using the oscilloscope.
Setup:
1. Open the PSLab Oscilloscope.
2. In the Channels menu, select the 'MIC' checkbox.
3. The MIC channel utilizes the host operating system microphone (laptop/phone internal mic or 3.5mm headset jack) and streams real-time acoustic data independently of any PSLab USB hardware connection.
4. Set the Voltage Scale to +/- 0.5V or +/- 1.0V (acoustic signals are small, typically Vpp = 0.02V to 0.15V).
5. Set the Timebase to 2.0 ms/div to 10.0 ms/div.
6. Hum, whistle, or speak into the microphone. A periodic sinusoidal waveform will appear.
7. The live frequency readout will identify the dominant pitch (e.g. 261 Hz for Middle C, 440 Hz for Concert A, or 300-400 Hz for low voice harmonics).
8. Enable the Fourier Transform (FFT) checkbox to view the fundamental frequency peak and acoustic harmonics.

documents.title: Experiment: Powering an LED with Programmable Power Supply
documents.content:
Experiment Guide: Powering an LED
Goal: Safely light and control the brightness of a Light Emitting Diode (LED) using programmable power sources.
Materials: PSLab board, standard LED (Red, Green, or White), 330 Ohm current-limiting resistor, jumper wires.
Circuit Wiring:
1. Connect PSLab PV1 pin to the resistor (330 Ohm).
2. Connect the other end of the resistor to the LED Anode (longer leg).
3. Connect the LED Cathode (shorter leg with flat rim) to PSLab GND pin.
Procedure:
1. Open the Power Source instrument in the PSLab app.
2. Set PV1 to 0.0V.
3. Gradually increase PV1 in 0.2V increments. Observe that the LED remains off until PV1 reaches the diode forward threshold (~1.8V for Red, ~3.0V for White/Blue).
4. As voltage increases past the forward threshold, the current begins flowing and brightness increases.

documents.title: Experiment: Operational Amplifier (Op-Amp) Inverting & Non-Inverting Amplifiers
documents.content:
Experiment Guide: Op-Amp Inverting Amplifier
Goal: Build and test an operational amplifier circuit to verify closed-loop voltage gain \(A_v = -\frac{R_f}{R_{\text{in}}}\).
Materials: PSLab board, LM358 or TL072 Op-Amp IC, two resistors (Rin = 10 kOhm, Rf = 47 kOhm), jumper wires.
Circuit Wiring:
1. Power rails: Connect PSLab PV1 (+5V) to Op-Amp Vcc+ pin, and PSLab GND to Op-Amp Vcc- pin.
2. Connect non-inverting input (+) to GND.
3. Connect input signal from PSLab Wave Generator W1 pin through Rin (10 kOhm) to inverting input (-).
4. Connect feedback resistor Rf (47 kOhm) between Op-Amp output and inverting input (-).
5. Measurement probes: Connect PSLab CH1 to W1 (input wave) and PSLab CH2 to Op-Amp output.
Procedure:
1. In Wave Generator, set W1 to 1000 Hz Sine Wave with 0.2V amplitude.
2. Open Oscilloscope, enable CH1 and CH2.
3. Observe that CH2 (output) is amplified by a factor of 4.7x and is 180 degrees out of phase with CH1 (input), confirming inverting amplifier theory.

documents.title: Experiment: RC Circuit Transient Response & Time Constant Tau
documents.content:
Experiment Guide: RC Circuit Transient Response
Goal: Measure the charging and discharging exponential curve of an RC low-pass filter and determine the time constant \(\tau = R \cdot C\).
Materials: PSLab board, 10 kOhm resistor, 0.1 uF ceramic/film capacitor, jumper wires.
Circuit Wiring:
1. Connect PSLab SQ1 (digital square wave output) to one side of the 10 kOhm resistor.
2. Connect the other side of the resistor to the positive terminal of the 0.1 uF capacitor and to PSLab CH1.
3. Connect the negative terminal of the capacitor to PSLab GND.
Procedure:
1. In Wave Generator, set SQ1 to a 100 Hz Square Wave with 50% duty cycle.
2. In Oscilloscope, select CH1, set Trigger to SQ1 Rising Edge, and set Timebase to 0.5 ms/div.
3. Observe the characteristic exponential curve: \(V(t) = V_{\max}(1 - e^{-t / \tau})\).
4. Theoretical tau = 10,000 Ohm * 0.0000001 F = 1.0 ms. Verify on screen that the voltage reaches 63.2% of peak at exactly 1.0 ms.

documents.title: Experiment: Diode I-V Characteristics & Zener Voltage Regulation
documents.content:
Experiment Guide: Diode Forward & Reverse Characteristics
Goal: Trace forward voltage drop and evaluate Zener diode breakdown voltage.
Materials: 1N4148 Silicon Diode or 3.3V Zener Diode, 1 kOhm current limiter, PSLab board.
Wiring:
1. Connect PSLab PCS (Programmable Constant Current Source) to the diode anode.
2. Connect diode cathode to GND.
3. Connect PSLab CH1 to the anode to measure voltage across the diode.
Procedure:
1. In Power Source, increase PCS current from 0.1 mA to 3.0 mA in steps.
2. Observe that the voltage measured by CH1 clamps around 0.65V to 0.72V, demonstrating the exponential forward diode characteristic.
3. For a Zener diode in reverse bias: connect PV1 through a 1 kOhm resistor to the Zener cathode, and Zener anode to GND. Ramp PV1 up to 5V; observe that the cathode voltage clamps tightly at the Zener rating (e.g. 3.3V).

documents.title: Sound Meter Architecture & Decibel Measurement
documents.content:
The PSLab Sound Meter instrument measures ambient sound pressure levels (SPL) in decibels (dB SPL). Key features and hardware notes:
• Audio Input: Operates directly via the host device's built-in microphone or an external microphone connected to the 3.5mm audio jack. Like the Oscilloscope MIC channel, the Sound Meter runs independently of the physical PSLab hardware board and can be used on standalone computers and phones.
• Decibel Scale: Sound levels are calculated as RMS sound pressure relative to the reference threshold of human hearing (0 dB SPL = 20 µPa). Typical ambient indoor noise is 30–45 dB SPL, normal conversational speech is 60–65 dB SPL, traffic noise is 75–85 dB SPL, and sounds above 85 dB SPL can cause hearing damage over prolonged exposure.
• Sound Classification Engine: Features built-in audio classification that tags sound events (such as speech, clapping, music, whistles, or motor noise) alongside live decibel logging.
• Logging & Export: Supports recording time-series sound level charts with GPS geolocation tags and exporting to CSV/TXT.

documents.title: Lux Meter Illuminance Measurement (BH1750, TSL2561, Ambient)
documents.content:
The PSLab Lux Meter measures ambient illuminance in units of Lux (lumens per square meter):
• Hardware Sensors: Supports external I2C digital light sensors including the BH1750 (0.11 to 100,000 Lux) and TSL2561 (high dynamic range with dual IR/visible diodes), as well as the host mobile device's ambient light sensor.
• Reference Values: Moonless night is ~0.001 Lux, living room lighting is 50–150 Lux, office workspace is 300–500 Lux, overcast day is 1,000–2,000 Lux, and direct full sunlight exceeds 30,000–100,000 Lux.
• Inverse Square Law Experiment: Used to empirically verify that light intensity decreases inversely with the square of distance from a point source: \(E = \frac{I}{d^2}\).

documents.title: Barometer & Altimeter (BMP180, Atmospheric Pressure)
documents.content:
The PSLab Barometer measures atmospheric air pressure in hectopascals (hPa) and calculates barometric altitude in meters:
• Hardware Sensors: Interfaces via I2C to BMP180 or BMP280 precision barometric sensors, or accesses the host device's internal barometer.
• Barometric Formula: Altitude is computed using the international standard barometric formula: \(h = 44330 \cdot \Big(1 - \big(\frac{P}{P_0}\big)^{\frac{1}{5.255}}\Big)\), where \(P_0\) is standard sea-level pressure (1013.25 hPa).
• Temperature Sensor: BMP180 also provides calibrated ambient temperature readings alongside pressure.

documents.title: Accelerometer 3-Axis Motion & G-Force (MPU6050, MPU9250)
documents.content:
The PSLab Accelerometer measures static acceleration due to gravity and dynamic acceleration due to motion along X, Y, and Z axes (in m/s^2 or g-force, 1g = 9.81 m/s^2):
• Hardware Sensors: Supports external 6-DoF/9-DoF IMUs (MPU6050, MPU9250) connected to PSLab I2C header pins, as well as host device internal accelerometers.
• Tilt & Inclination Formulas: Pitch and Roll angles are computed from linear acceleration components: \(\text{pitch} = \arctan\!\Big(\frac{A_x}{\sqrt{A_y^2 + A_z^2}}\Big)\) and \(\text{roll} = \arctan\!\Big(\frac{A_y}{\sqrt{A_x^2 + A_z^2}}\Big)\).
• Experiments: Inclination, harmonic pendulum oscillations, vehicle acceleration, and mechanical vibration analysis.

documents.title: Gyroscope Angular Velocity & Rotation (MPU6050, MPU9250)
documents.content:
The PSLab Gyroscope measures the rate of rotation about X, Y, and Z axes in radians per second (rad/s) or degrees per second (deg/s):
• Hardware Sensors: Utilizes MEMS vibrating structure gyroscopes via MPU6050 or MPU9250 on the I2C bus.
• Applications: Inertial navigation, measuring centripetal acceleration on rotating turntables, and complementary filter sensor fusion combining accelerometer and gyroscope data.

documents.title: Electronic Compass & Magnetometer (HMC5883L)
documents.content:
The PSLab Compass measures Earth's geomagnetic field vector components (in micro-Tesla, µT) and calculates azimuth heading (0 to 360 degrees):
• Hardware Sensors: Interfaces to the Honeywell HMC5883L 3-axis digital magnetometer or internal device magnetometers.
• Heading Computation: Azimuth angle is computed via atan2(Y, X) corrected for tilt pitch and roll angles from the accelerometer: \(\text{heading} = \arctan2(Y_h, X_h) \cdot \frac{180}{\pi}\).
• Experiments: Mapping magnetic fields around permanent magnets, Helmholtz coils, and current-carrying solenoids.

documents.title: Digital Thermometer & Environmental Temperature (SHT21, LM35)
documents.content:
The PSLab Thermometer measures ambient and surface temperatures:
• Hardware Sensors: Supports digital Sensirion SHT21 humidity/temperature sensors via I2C, analog LM35/TMP36 sensors connected to PSLab CH1/CH3 analog inputs (10 mV/°C linear scale), or host device thermal sensors.
• Experiments: Newton's law of cooling, thermal equilibrium between liquids, and temperature coefficient of resistance (TCR) of copper wire.

documents.title: Gas Sensor & Air Quality Monitoring (MQ Series, MQ-2, MQ-135)
documents.content:
The PSLab Gas Sensor instrument evaluates concentrations of combustible gases, smoke, and air quality pollutants:
• Hardware Sensors: Interfaces with metal-oxide semiconductor (MOS) sensors like MQ-2 (LPG, propane, methane, smoke) and MQ-135 (air quality, NH3, NOx, benzene, CO2) connected to PSLab analog inputs.
• Operation & Preheating: MOS gas sensors require internal heating coil power (5V from PSLab PV1/Vdd) and need 1–3 minutes preheating to reach stable baseline resistance (R0).
• Reading Modes: Raw voltage (0–3.3V) and logarithmic Parts Per Million (PPM) concentration curves based on Rs/R0 ratio.

documents.title: OLED Graphic Display Controller (SSD1306, SH1106)
documents.content:
The PSLab OLED Display instrument drives monochrome graphic OLED screens:
• Hardware Specifications: Supports 0.96-inch 128x64 pixel SSD1306 and SH1106 controller displays over the PSLab I2C bus at address 0x3C or 0x3D.
• Modes: Interactive drawing canvas, real-time bitmap graphics rendering, animated GIF playback, and built-in interactive mini-games.
• Wiring: Connect PSLab 3.3V/VDD to OLED VCC, GND to GND, SCL to SCL, and SDA to SDA.

documents.title: PSLab Project History, Origins, and Production Milestones
documents.content:
Pocket Science Lab (PSLab) History, Origins, and Major Milestones:
• The Beginnings (2014 FOSSASIA Summit in Cambodia):
  - At the FOSSASIA Summit 2014 in Cambodia, open-source developers met to discuss creating Open Source Hardware. Praveen Kumar proposed further developing the 'Sealablet' hardware and creating dedicated software for it.
  - The team initiated discussions with Jithin B.P., the original developer of the Sealablet. At the time, open-source hardware was still a novel concept.
  - Jithin generously agreed to release an adapted version of his hardware as Open Source under the FOSSASIA organization and subsequently joined FOSSASIA as a Google Summer of Code (GSoC) student to build the initial foundation.
• Mobile Revolution & Form Factor Evolution (2017):
  - In 2017, FOSSASIA launched development of the native PSLab Android application. This enabled educators, students, and hobbyists to conduct real science and electronics experiments using handheld smartphones without requiring a desktop computer.
  - The hardware form factor was redesigned into a compact pocket-sized form factor, onboard components were modernized, and dedicated sockets for an ESP-01 Wi-Fi module and Bluetooth were incorporated. These improvements reduced production costs while expanding real-world usability.
• Mass Production in Shenzhen (October 2018):
  - After extensive hardware iterations, rapid prototypes, and Android Beta testing, the first large commercial production batch of 1,000 Pocket Science Lab boards was manufactured in Shenzhen, China in October 2018.
• International Market Launch & Worldwide Adoption:
  - PSLab was first introduced commercially in Japan to the Maker community, where the entire first shipment sold out on its second day.
  - Retail distribution subsequently launched through the Singapore store, followed by official availability in European Union, United States, and Chinese markets.
• Cross-Platform Evolution (Flutter & Rust):
  - The software ecosystem evolved from platform-specific code to a unified, high-performance cross-platform application built with Flutter for the user interface and a Rust-based serial communication backend using FFI, supporting Android, Desktop (Linux, macOS, Windows), Web, and iOS.

documents.title: PSLab Vision, Open Science Mission, and Development Architecture
documents.content:
PSLab Vision, Technical Architecture, and Open Science Ecosystem:
• The Vision: Miniaturizing Laboratories for Everyone:
  - PSLab was created to miniaturize bulky, expensive laboratory equipment into an affordable, pocket-sized device accessible to students, teachers, researchers, and citizen scientists worldwide.
  - Enables independent experimentation and data collection to verify real-world phenomena (e.g. air quality, acoustic spectra, circuit characteristics) with replicable, trustworthy, 100% open-source tools.
  - Licensed under the Apache License 2.0; all layers (hardware schematics, firmware, mobile app, desktop app) can be inspected, modified, and built from scratch.
• Organizational Homes:
  - Proudly developed by FOSSASIA (Singapore) and OpnTec (Germany) together with a worldwide community.
• Technical Software Architecture:
  - Frontend (Flutter & Dart): Provides a reactive UI, cross-platform state management, and unified instrument views.
  - Hardware Communication (Rust): Low-level serial communication and high-speed data stream processing are implemented in Rust, connected to Flutter via Foreign Function Interface (FFI). This ensures near bare-metal performance, thread safety, and zero garbage-collection jitter.
• Platform Compatibility Matrix:
  - Android: Primary platform. Connects via USB OTG or Wi-Fi (ESP-01) for PSLab; USB OTG for Labrador; supports in-app Firmware Flashing via USB cable.
  - Desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux): USB serial and Web support for PSLab and Labrador; supports Firmware Flashing via USB cable.
  - Web (WebUSB / WebSerial): In-browser instrument control and firmware flashing.
  - iOS: Supports official PSLab board strictly over Wi-Fi via ESP-01 module. iOS DOES NOT support EspoTek Labrador. iOS DOES NOT support firmware flashing.
• Where to Order & Contribute:
  - Official Shop: https://pslab.io/shop/ (available in European Union, USA, Singapore, and Japan).
  - Code Repositories on GitHub: fossasia/pslab-app, fossasia/pslab-hardware, fossasia/pslab-firmware, fossasia/pslab-esp01-firmware.
  - Translations: Managed on Weblate (hosted.weblate.org/projects/fossasia/pslab-app/).
  - Communication: Gitter channel at gitter.im/fossasia/pslab and Google Groups mailing list.

documents.title: PSLab Application Software Architecture: Flutter UI & Rust Backend Communication
documents.content:
PSLab Application Architecture & Technical Implementation:
• High-Level Stack Summary: The modern unified Pocket Science Lab app (fossasia/pslab-app) is engineered using a two-tier architecture: Flutter (Dart) for the user interface and reactive state management, and Rust (rust_lib_pslab) for low-level backend communication, hardware drivers, and performance-critical signal processing.
• CRITICAL CLARIFICATION (NOT PYTHON): The modern PSLab app is NOT built with Python! Earlier historical tools from 2014–2018 included a legacy Python library (pslab-python) and a PyQt desktop utility. However, the current official PSLab multi-platform application is 100% written in Flutter + Rust. Python is NOT used anywhere in the codebase. Any assertion that the app uses Python, C++, or Java/Kotlin for its core logic is completely false.
• Frontend & UI Layer (Flutter / Dart):
  - Framework: Flutter with Dart, delivering a 60/120 FPS responsive UI across Android, iOS, Windows, macOS, Linux, and Web.
  - State Management: Provider pattern utilizing ChangeNotifier (e.g. OscilloscopeStateProvider, MultimeterStateProvider, PowerSourceStateProvider, BoardStateProvider, AiAssistantProvider) combined with the get_it service locator (locator.dart) for dependency injection.
  - UI Components: Material Design 3 theming with dynamic dark/light mode, custom high-performance charts via fl_chart, localization support for 18+ languages, and direct device sensor integration (accelerometer, gyroscope, barometer, compass, sound meter).
• Backend & Hardware Communication Layer (Rust):
  - Rust Crate (rust_lib_pslab): Implements the hardware abstraction layer, raw USB packet framing, serial bus protocols, checksum validation, and high-speed data stream parsing.
  - Bridging Layer: flutter_rust_bridge (FRB v2) generates zero-copy, asynchronous, thread-safe FFI bindings between Dart and Rust, guaranteeing near bare-metal speed with zero garbage-collection jitter.
  - Rust Subsystems:
    1. common.rs: Core PSLab protocol serialization, command packet assembly, and transaction queues.
    2. labrador.rs: High-throughput USB acquisition for the EspoTek Labrador oscilloscope at 750 kSPS, wave generator controls, and PSU switching.
    3. bootloader.rs & labrador_bootloader.rs: Intel HEX parsing (ihex crate), checksum verification, and safe in-app firmware flashing / DFU flashing over USB.
    4. audio.rs: Low-latency acoustic signal acquisition using cpal on desktop.
• Platform-Specific Hardware Implementation:
  - Android: Flutter UI + Android USB Host API / USB OTG driver (usb_serial) + compiled native Rust shared library (.so). Connects via USB OTG or Wi-Fi (ESP-01).
  - Desktop (Windows, macOS, Linux): Flutter Desktop + native Rust using rusb (vendored libusb) for raw USB and serialport for serial COM ports.
  - Web (Browsers): Flutter Web + Rust compiled to WebAssembly (wasm32-unknown-unknown via wasm-bindgen and web-sys), using the browser native WebSerial API for direct USB board connection.
  - iOS (iPhone / iPad): Flutter iOS + Wi-Fi TCP/IP socket handler (ios_comms_handler.dart, wifi_comms_handler.dart) connecting wirelessly to the ESP-01 module at 192.168.4.1. (Apple iOS strictly blocks raw USB OTG device communication; EspoTek Labrador and firmware flashing are unsupported on iOS).
